solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Man seemingly going to great lengths for poet (10)

blocks.note: something that goes to great lengths is long
surface padding: hints that the man's name reads as a description of him

annotation.surface: Someone describes a tall man who seems to stretch on forever.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Seemingly' signals that the man's name reads like a description: a long fellow. Henry Wadsworth Longfellow wrote The Song of Hiawatha.
annotation.definitionFit: Longfellow was a nineteenth-century American poet.

entries.clue: Animal rootled at first in poor soil (5)

indicatorNotes.at first: take only the first letter of 'rootled'
indicatorNotes.in: R goes inside the other letters
indicatorNotes.poor: soil in poor shape is rearranged

annotation.surface: An animal has been snuffling around in thin, poor soil.
annotation.walkthrough: The picture of a pig rooting in the dirt distracts from the fact that 'rootled' supplies just one letter; 'poor' is the anagram signal, not a comment on the soil.
annotation.definitionFit: A loris is a small, slow-moving tree-dwelling primate.

entries.clue: Enjoy wrestling with a sow? Absolutely not! (2,3,4)

indicatorNotes.wrestling: letters grappled into a new order

annotation.surface: Someone is asked whether they'd like to wrestle a pig, and firmly declines.
annotation.walkthrough: The question and its answer are one scene: the refusal is also the definition. 'No way, José' is a jokey rhyming way of saying no.
annotation.definitionFit: 'No way, José' is an emphatic informal refusal.

entries.clue: Love female struggling with 4 problems? (5)

blocks.note: 4 down is LEG; someone struggling with leg problems is lame

annotation.surface: A question about someone whose romantic partner has troubles.
annotation.walkthrough: The '4' points to the answer at 4 down, LEG, so the phrase means 'struggling with leg problems'.
annotation.definitionFit: An old flame is a former love, so a flame is a sweetheart.

entries.clue: Stage left for example (3)

annotation.surface: A theatre direction: stage left, as an example.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Stage left' reads as a theatre term, but 'Stage' stands alone as the definition and 'left' starts the wordplay.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a journey or relay race is split into sections, each one a stage.

entries.clue: Men network and party in Floridian resort (7)

blocks.note: OR = other ranks, soldiers who are not officers

annotation.surface: Men go networking and partying at a Florida holiday spot.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Men' as OR (other ranks) is a standard crossword convention worth learning.
annotation.definitionFit: Orlando in Florida is a resort city famous for its theme parks.

entries.clue: Man is free with plonk — light red? (6,4)

indicatorNotes.free: the letters are set free to rearrange

annotation.surface: A man is generous with cheap wine — perhaps a light red?
annotation.walkthrough: Plonk is British slang for cheap wine, so 'light red' seems to be a wine; it is really a colour.
annotation.definitionFit: Salmon pink is a pale orangey-pink colour, a light red of sorts, hence the question mark.

entries.clue: One sent from Bow in a right ding-dong (5)

blocks.note: a ding-dong is a heated argument, a row

annotation.surface: Someone from Bow, in London's East End, gets caught up in a proper quarrel.
annotation.walkthrough: The capital B makes Bow look like the London district; it is a bow that shoots arrows. A ding-dong is British slang for a noisy argument.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by description: the missile an archer looses from a bow.

entries.clue: Dancing along with an African (7)

indicatorNotes.Dancing: the letters move about into a new order

annotation.surface: Someone dances along with an African partner.
annotation.walkthrough: The dancer and the African share one scene, which keeps the anagram out of sight.
annotation.definitionFit: An Angolan is a person from Angola, in Africa.

entries.clue: Direct instruction Edward Lear disregarded? (2-8)

blocks.note: Lear was famous for absurd comic verse, so an order forbidding silliness is one he would ignore

annotation.surface: A plain order that the poet Edward Lear chose to ignore.
annotation.walkthrough: Edward Lear was a Victorian writer of nonsense verse, such as The Owl and the Pussy-cat. 'Direct' looks like a verb but is the adjective.
annotation.definitionFit: Direct in the sense of plain-speaking and businesslike; the second sense is a pun on Lear's comic verse.

entries.clue: Greek character she pays badly for dish (5,4)

indicatorNotes.badly: the letters are put together badly, out of order

blocks.note: mu is the Greek letter M

annotation.surface: A Greek character in a story pays poorly for a meal.
annotation.walkthrough: Mushy peas are a British side dish of mashed marrowfat peas, served with fish and chips. 'Character' here is a letter, not a person.
annotation.definitionFit: Mushy peas are a dish in their own right, a classic chip-shop side.

entries.clue: Contemplate large drink or experience its effect? (3,6)

blocks.note: a double is a large measure of spirits

annotation.surface: Weighing up a big drink, or feeling what it does to you.
annotation.walkthrough: The wordplay and the definition both describe drinking: too many doubles and you see double.
annotation.definitionFit: Seeing double, blurred vision, is the effect of too much drink.

entries.clue: Nothing to say for sister (3)

indicatorNotes.to say: spoken, it gives the sound of the word

blocks.note: none = nothing, as in 'there is none left', said aloud

annotation.surface: Someone has nothing to say on behalf of their sister.
annotation.walkthrough: A 'sister' is a nun, a member of a religious order, not a sibling.
annotation.definitionFit: A title sense: women in a religious order are addressed as Sister.

entries.clue: Scientist unfamiliar with nitrogen? (6)

blocks.note: N is the chemical symbol for nitrogen

annotation.surface: A scientist who has never met nitrogen.
annotation.walkthrough: 'with' looks like a link but belongs to the phrase: unfamiliar with = NEW TO.
annotation.definitionFit: Isaac Newton was the great English physicist and mathematician.

entries.clue: Defensive structure great for Scots hero (7)

annotation.surface: A splendid fortification built for a Scottish champion.
annotation.walkthrough: William Wallace led the Scots against England around 1300 and was the hero of the film Braveheart.
annotation.definitionFit: William Wallace is a Scottish national hero.

entries.clue: Reputation British sailors have around east (6)

indicatorNotes.around: 'around' means surrounding, so the sailors' letters are wrapped about the E

annotation.surface: The Royal Navy has a reputation that stretches all the way east.
annotation.walkthrough: Although 'around' stands next to 'have', the E goes inside the Royal Navy's initials, not inside the verb.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: fame earned by deeds is a good reputation.

entries.clue: Evil one Lionel disheartened (3)

indicatorNotes.disheartened: the heart, the middle letters, is removed

annotation.surface: A wicked person called Lionel has lost heart.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Evil one' looks like a phrase for a villain, but 'one' belongs to the wordplay.
annotation.definitionFit: Ill as a noun means evil, harm, as in 'speak no ill'.

entries.clue: Crackers are able to expand (9)

indicatorNotes.Crackers: crackers = crazy, so the letters go mad

annotation.surface: Biscuits that can swell up.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Crackers' reads as a noun, biscuits, but works as the adjective crazy, a British informal word.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to add detail to an idea is to expand on it.

entries.clue: Measureless chasm in area near steamship (5)

annotation.surface: A bottomless ocean trench in waters close to a steamship.
annotation.walkthrough: 'in' looks like it puts something inside, but it only joins the definition to the wordplay.
annotation.definitionFit: An abyss is a chasm too deep to measure.

entries.clue: A trotter possibly for cooking? (5)

blocks.note: a trotter is a pig's hoofed extremity, one example of what you stand on; 'possibly' flags the example

annotation.surface: A pig's trotter, perhaps destined for the pot.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Cooking' seems to follow on from trotter, but it means 'going on', as in 'what's cooking?'.
annotation.definitionFit: Something afoot is under way, just as something cooking is being plotted or happening.

entries.clue: King backed an extremely wicked activity (7)

indicatorNotes.backed: AN is turned back to front

annotation.surface: A monarch supported some thoroughly wicked deed.
annotation.walkthrough: 'backed' reads as 'supported', but here it turns round only the AN that follows it.
annotation.definitionFit: Knavery is the dishonest behaviour of a knave, a rogue.

entries.clue: Long dashes in eastern manuscript (3)

annotation.surface: Long dashes appear in an old eastern manuscript.
annotation.walkthrough: The em dash is the long dash of printing; in typesetters' jargon an em is both the width and the dash itself.
annotation.definitionFit: Ems are long dashes, each as wide as the letter M.

entries.clue: Blasts waste by son (5)

blocks.note: to blow money is to waste it

annotation.surface: Explosions of rubbish set off by someone's son.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Waste' reads as a noun, rubbish, but it is the verb: to blow money.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: hard strikes, or gusts of wind, can both be called blasts.

entries.clue: Endless parking in streets regulated (10)

indicatorNotes.regulated: the letters are put into a new order

blocks.note: P = parking, as on road signs

annotation.surface: Complaints about never-ending parking rules on city streets.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Endless' looks like a deletion signal, cut the last letter, but it is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: Something persistent goes on and on without end.
